summary:
Sexual relations between people of the same sex are lawful in Liechtenstein. Anti-discrimination law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are covered by no anti-discrimination statute in force, so a trans visitor has no protected ground to invoke in a discrimination complaint. No law in the sources reviewed prohibits intersex genital modification.

Penal protection runs along the sexual-orientation axis. Since 1 April 2016 harassment and incitement to hatred on grounds of sexual orientation have been banned. Section 283(1) of the Penal Code punishes public incitement to hatred or discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation with up to two years' imprisonment, and section 283(6) prohibits discrimination in public facilities on the same grounds. The Media Act of October 2005 declares media content illegal where it incites or supports discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. These grounds turn on sexual orientation; no equivalent provision on gender identity or gender expression is recorded.

Liechtenstein has no procedure for changing a legal gender marker in official documents, so no identity document issued there can be made to match a person's gender. A traveller arriving on documents issued elsewhere is not affected by Liechtenstein practice in respect of those documents, but anyone who depends on Liechtenstein-issued identification, or who stays in the country, cannot obtain a marker consistent with their gender.

No law in force restricts access to sex-segregated facilities on the basis of gender identity.

Marriage has been open since January 2025 to couples regardless of gender or sexual orientation, and joint adoption is available on the same terms. A trans visitor in a relationship that Liechtenstein would class by birth-sex status can therefore marry there, and the marriage would be recognised as such domestically.

Official posture has been less protective than the statutes. The Roman Catholic Church is the state religion, and the archbishop publicly opposed marriage equality. In a January 2016 New Year interview Prince Hans-Adam II described rainbow families as irresponsible, said children have a right to a normal family, and suggested Liechtenstein could ignore an adverse ruling from the European Court of Human Rights. The LGBT organisation Flay said the remarks left it shocked, and the Freie Liste called them contrary to the Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights.
tangentialFactors:
Registered partnership was the pivot of the marriage debate. A September 2022 Landtag motion, Motion zur Öffnung der Ehe für alle, asked the legislature to open civil marriage regardless of gender and sexual orientation and to remove the remaining legal differences between partnership and marriage; it recorded that registered partners were seen as holding a second-class marriage. Prince Hans-Adam II had said in 2021 that he had nothing against marriage equality except adoption. The opening of civil marriage and joint adoption followed in January 2025.

Community infrastructure is thin. With a population of roughly 35,000 there is no organised gay scene, and friendship networks serve that function. A 2012 country account recorded few organised opponents, listing no religious extremists, no right-wing skinheads and no political figures campaigning for homophobic laws, and described gay people as living comfortably with little interference. That assessment predates the marriage debate and the first Pride, held in 2022.
localsOnly:
The Stabsstelle für Chancengleichheit (Department of Equal Opportunities) was assigned on 22 February 2005 to take discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation into its remit. The mandate names sexual orientation; the sources record no extension of it to gender identity or gender expression. There is no gender identity ground a resident can bring to that office.

For residents, marriage and joint adoption have been available since January 2025. Registered partnerships concluded earlier remain in force, and no procedure exists for a resident to change a gender marker on a Liechtenstein identity document.
outOfScopeNotes:
A Reuters feature on small European states and LGBT equality could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 401), so any material it contains is not reflected here.

The sources reviewed report no prosecution, complaint or enforcement data under section 283 of the Penal Code or under the Media Act. Whether the criminal provisions are applied in practice is unresolved.

The absence of a rule on sex-segregated facilities follows from the absence of any gender-identity legislation. No source reviewed states a facilities rule in positive terms.

The account of everyday social conditions dates from 2012 and has not been re-verified against later sources.
